cases.name: allow-with-no-opinion
cases.note: No rule speaks for this action, so the engine's default holds.

cases.name: block-names-the-triggering-argument
cases.note: attributed_to is the argument NAME ('path'). The value (/etc/passwd) must not appear in any field of the decision, which is why this case also asserts the absence of the value.

cases.name: block-with-no-attribution
cases.note: deny_tool denies a whole action; there is no argument to name.

cases.name: modify-replaces-a-non-dict-result
cases.note: A non-dict result rides the event under the 'result' key (interceptors.mcp wraps it that way), so the rule can name 'result' as what it reacted to.

cases.name: modify-replaces-a-dict-result
cases.note: A dict result is carried as itself, not wrapped - the two shapes must not be conflated across the wire.

cases.name: bytes-survive-the-round-trip
cases.note: JSON has no bytes. A binary result replaced by a rule must arrive as the same bytes, not as a string or a lossy repr.

cases.name: a-set-is-normalised-to-a-sorted-list
cases.note: JSON has no set either, and unlike bytes a set is represented rather than escaped: sorted, so the same set always serialises the same way.

cases.name: a-null-replacement-means-no-replacement
cases.note: A rule returning modified_result=None has asked for no replacement, which is how the in-process path reads it too (interceptors.mcp applies a MODIFY result only when it is not None). The wire invents no semantics Python lacks.

cases.name: an-untransmittable-rewrite-is-refused
cases.note: A rule rewrote the result to a value with no JSON form. The daemon cannot say what it decided, so it says so: an error frame, which the client must treat as a block. Silently dropping the rewrite would return the unredacted payload.

cases.name: call-side-rules-do-not-judge-results
cases.note: The same action name at phase='result' must not trip the call-side rules that deny read_file. Two rules on one action name make the phase partition observable from outside.

cases.name: principal-crosses-the-wire
cases.note: A rule reads event.principal; a wire that drops it changes the verdict.

cases.name: parent-principal-crosses-the-wire
cases.note: parent_principal is the delegation field - the one a spawned-principal rule consults and the one easiest to forget in a hand-written protocol.

negatives.name: unknown-protocol-version
negatives.note: A version the daemon does not speak is refused, not guessed at.

negatives.name: misspelled-args-key-is-refused-not-ignored
negatives.note: 'arg' is not 'args'. Dropping it silently would show the engine an event with no arguments - and an engine with no opinion allows.

negatives.name: missing-args-is-refused
negatives.note: Absent arguments are refused rather than defaulted to an empty object.

negatives.name: args-must-be-an-object
negatives.note: A list where an object belongs is a client bug worth surfacing.

negatives.name: phase-is-case-sensitive
negatives.note: 'Result' is not 'result'; accepting it would silently run a result rule as call-side.

negatives.name: unknown-event-key-is-refused
negatives.note: An unrecognised key is a typo the far end cannot see; refusing makes it visible.

negatives.name: missing-id-is-refused
negatives.note: Without an id a response cannot be matched to its request.

negatives.name: oversized-frame-is-refused
negatives.note: The size check runs before parsing, so a frame over the limit is refused without being parsed. The reader cannot report unrepresentable types in the decisions it is asked about. The connection is then closed.
